title: What is known about 1RB0RF_1RC1RF_1LD0LE_---1LC_1RA1LE_1LC1RB
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0RF_1RC1RF_1LD0LE_---1LC_1RA1LE_1LC1RB.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: Open, reduced in Lean to a Collatz-like map, probviously non-halting. The tape is always, at the end of a pass, one block of n ones. The pass sends n to f(n), where f depends on the power of two dividing n+2; the machine halts exactly when the orbit of 4 reaches an n with n+2 a power of two. All of this is proved in Lean for every n (halts_iff, f_none_iff), and the orbit of 4 avoids the halting values for 10,000 passes in Lean and 200,000 in exact arithmetic. The low bits of the orbit behave like random bits, and on that model the chance of ever halting is about 2−80,000.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (D0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 26,681 cells have been visited and 26,679 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Blank tape reaches P(4)
claims.text: After 9 steps the tape is a single block of four 1s with the head, in state B, on the blank cell to its right: P(4) = 0^inf 1^4 B> 0^inf.

claims.title: Every pass, for every n
claims.text: Write X(a, b, c) for 0^inf 1^a E> 0 1^b 0 1^c 0^inf. P(n+1) reaches X(0, n, 2), and from X(0, b, c) the machine halts or reaches P(g(b, c)) with g(0, c) = c+2 (c even) or (3c+9)/2 (c odd), g(2i+2, c) = c+3i+5, g(1, c) = halt, g(2i+3, c) = g(i, c+i+4). So the pass from P(n) ends at P(f(n)), f(n) = g(n−1, 2), or halts. Proved for all n from 17 symtm rules (an odd zigzag, an even zigzag, their ends) and inductions.

claims.title: Halts iff the orbit of 4 hits a halting value
claims.text: The machine halts from blank tape if and only if the orbit of 4 under f reaches none; and f(n) is none exactly when n+2 is a power of two, at least 4.

claims.title: The odd pass in closed form
claims.text: P(2k+3) reaches P(3k+7): n ↦ (3n+5)/2 on odd n (the first, separate proof).

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 passes
claims.text: The orbit of 4 under the Lean function f is evaluated by compiled code for 10,000 passes and never reaches none.

claims.title: Closed form, and 200,000 passes
claims.text: Writing n+2 = 2<sup>j</sup>m with m odd, f(n) = 2<sup>j</sup>m + (m+2j−1)/2, except m = 1 (halt) and m = 3 with j even and ≥ 2 (f(n) = 9·2<sup>j−1</sup> + 3j/2 + 3); checked against g for every n < 200,000 and against direct simulation of passes for n ≤ 3000. Iterating f from 4 for 200,000 passes (exact integers) never halts; n then has 80,223 bits.

claims.title: The low bits look random
claims.text: Over the 200,000 passes the counts of j = v<sub>2</sub>(n+2) follow the geometric law 2<sup>−(j+1)</sup> (99,772 / 100,000 for j = 0, 50,060 / 50,000 for j = 1, 25,207 / 25,000 for j = 2, …; largest j = 17), and n grows by e<sup>0.2780</sup> per pass against e<sup>0.2783</sup> predicted for random low bits.

claims.title: Only two kinds of pass can lead to a halt
claims.text: A short argument (not in Lean): f(n)+2 = 2<sup>k</sup> needs m(2<sup>j+1</sup>+1) + 2j + 3 = 2<sup>k+1</sup> (or the m = 3 exception, which never gives a power of two). Since 2<sup>j+1</sup> ≡ −1 modulo 2<sup>j+1</sup>+1, the powers of two are ±2<sup>i</sup> there, and 2j+3 is one of these only for j = 2 (9m+7 = 2<sup>k+1</sup>) and j = 3 (17m+9 = 2<sup>k+1</sup>). So halting values have about 1.3 preimage-or-self per binary length, among 2<sup>L</sup> numbers.

claims.title: Probviously never halts
claims.text: The orbit gains about 0.40 bits per pass, so it spends about 2.5 passes per binary length, each with a chance of about 2<sup>−L</sup> to land on one of those values. From 80,223 bits on, the expected number of halts left is about 2<sup>−80,000</sup>. No invariant forbidding a halt is known: the residues of the orbit look equidistributed.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Exactly when the orbit 4, 8, 13, 22, 28, … of f (defined and proved in Lean) reaches an n with n+2 a power of two. This is a Collatz-type question; a proof of non-halting would need control of the low bits of the orbit forever.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows, but the question is now a clean one about numbers. At the end of every pass the tape is one block of n ones; the next pass turns n into f(n), and the machine stops exactly when n+2 is a power of two. This page shows the passes, the map and why it is hard.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 26,681 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
The pass on odd n, proved for every odd n ≥ 3.
The pass map f, proved for every n; the machine halts iff the orbit of 4 hits such an n.
Chance that the orbit ever halts, if its low bits are random.

sections.heading: One block of ones, and a map on its length
html: Watch the run for a while and one picture keeps coming back: the whole tape is one block of n ones, and the head, in state B, has just stepped off its right end onto a blank cell. Call that configuration P(n). The run from blank tape reaches P(4) after 9 steps, and then P(8), P(13), P(22), P(28), P(38), P(45), P(70), … Between two of these, the machine makes a pass: about 1.3·n2 steps of sweeping back and forth inside the block.
So the whole question is what the pass does to n. It depends on the low binary digits of n+2.
Odd n: one zigzag

If n is odd, B runs left to the far end, writes a single 0 three cells in, and the head starts a zigzag that pushes that 0 back to the right, two cells per round, while the block on its left grows by three. When the 0 falls off the right end the tape is one block again, of length (3n+5)/2. This is proved in Lean for every odd n ≥ 3.

steptape
3,3831^45 B>
3,6591^3 0 1^44 C>
3,9221^6 0 1^42 C>
……
6,6621^66 0 1^2 C>
6,6691^70 B>
In general: two zigzags

Write X(a, b, c) for the tape 1^a E> 0 1^b 0 1^c: three blocks of ones separated by two 0s, the head at the left end. Every pass starts with P(n+1) → X(0, n, 2). Then the parity of the middle block b decides:

• b odd: each round moves one 1 from the middle block to each side, X(a, b, c) → X(a+1, b−2, c+1), until b = 1; then X(a+1, 1, c) → X(0, a, c+3): the left block becomes the new middle block, which is (b−3)/2. If a = 0 here, state D reads a 0 and the machine halts.
  • b even: the right block is moved to the left one cell at a time, X(a, b, c) → X(a+c, b, 0), and then each round turns two cells of the middle block into three on the left, until X(a′, 0, 2), which is one block again: P(c + 3b/2 + 2). (For b = 0 and c odd the pass goes once more through 1^m F>.)

So with B = b+3 the odd case halves B, and the machine halts when B reaches 4. Starting from B = n+2, it halts exactly when n+2 is a power of two. All of this is proved in Lean for every n, with the exact map. Writing n+2 = 2j·m with m odd, the pass ends with
f(n) = 2j·m + (m + 2j − 1)/2

(for odd n this is j = 0 and f(n) = (3n+5)/2), with two exceptions: if m = 1, that is n+2 is a power of two, the halving runs out of room and the machine halts (state D reads a 0); if m = 3 and j is even, the last halving wraps around and f(n) = 9·2j−1 + 3j/2 + 3. This closed form agrees with the Lean map for every n < 200,000 and with direct simulation for n ≤ 3000.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.497).
After 109 steps the tape spans 26,681 cells (41 left of the start, 19,927 right), with a density of 1s of 1.0.

The tape (run-length coded, 1^5 is five 1s, C>0 the head in state C on a 0) at some of the last moments the head reached a new cell, cut to 400 characters:

sidesteptape
right954,638,5001^18138 0 1^7290 C>0
right970,277,5911^19269 0 1^6536 C>0
right985,930,9841^20550 0 1^5682 C>0
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: A Collatz-like question
html: The machine halts if and only if the orbit 4 → 8 → 13 → 22 → … ever lands on a number n with n+2 a power of two (proved in Lean: halts_iff). The map multiplies by about 3/2 when n is odd, by about 1 + 2−j−1 otherwise, and the next j depends on the low bits of the result: the same mix of multiplication and binary digits that makes the Collatz problem hard. Nobody knows how to prove that such an orbit avoids a thin set like {2k − 2} forever.

Heuristically it does: on average n gains 0.40 bits per pass, and the chance that a number near n is two less than a power of two is about 1/n. After 200,000 passes of the formula, n has 80,223 bits and the orbit never came close.

summary: One block of n ones; each pass maps n to about n(1+2^-(j+1)), j the 2-adic valuation of n+2, and it halts iff n+2 is ever a power of two.
family: Collatz-like map on one block length (2-adic halving bouncer)
